clue.text: Exercise where pervert bites character in the Cyclades

indicators.note: something that bites holds another piece between its jaws, so one word closes round the other

parts.note: to pervert is to warp or distort
the Cyclades are Greek islands, so a character there is a Greek letter, mu

explanation.surface: A gym session somewhere a deviant is chewing on a Greek islander.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bites' signals a container: the warped word closes its jaws round the Greek character. 'pervert' looks like a noun but is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: A loosening-up session before sport is a form of exercise, a synonym in the gym sense.

clue.text: Word of regret, detailing something possibly mixed up

indicators.note: letters mixed up are jumbled into a new order
de-tailing means docking the tail, the final letter

parts.note: a salad is an example of something that is mixed up, hence 'possibly'

explanation.surface: A sigh of sorrow while giving the details of some muddle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'detailing' cuts the tail D from SALAD to leave SALA, which 'mixed up' rearranges. 'Detailing' looks like 'explaining' but means docking.
explanation.definitionFit: This interjection voices sorrow or regret, so it is literally a word of regret.

clue.text: Midlife crisis where people work to accept a regrettable conclusion?

parts.note: men is a common crossword word for people

indicators.note: a word that accepts another takes it inside itself

parts.note: an opus is a musical or literary work

indicators.note: the conclusion of a word is its final letter

explanation.surface: A workplace where staff take on a sorry ending, suggesting a midlife meltdown.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to accept' puts A inside OPUS; 'conclusion' takes the E ending regrettable. The question mark flags that this crisis is biological.
explanation.definitionFit: The change of life arrives in midlife and is often jokingly treated as a crisis, an apt rather than dictionary sense.

clue.text: General arrangement under discussion

indicators.note: something under discussion is being spoken about, so the word is judged by how it is said

parts.note: a pattern is an arrangement or design

explanation.surface: A broad layout is being debated in a meeting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'General' looks like an adjective but is the military rank: George Patton was a US general in the Second World War.
explanation.definitionFit: George S. Patton was a celebrated American army commander of the Second World War.

clue.text: Quest for adventure the Queen managed to attempt

parts.note: ER, Elizabeth Regina, is the Queen's royal cipher
to run a business is to manage it
a try is an attempt

explanation.surface: The monarch succeeded in having a go at some daring escapade.
explanation.definitionFit: Knight-errantry is the wandering of a knight in search of adventure, the word's literal sense.

clue.text: Rocky Marciano and me talk about where the treasure's hidden!

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the jumbled letters go round the next piece
rocky means unsteady, so these letters are shaken into a new order

parts.note: on a pirate map, X marks the spot of buried treasure

explanation.surface: A boxer and I chat about the location of buried loot, excitedly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rocky' signals the anagram and 'about' the container. The definition is the printed punctuation mark at the end. Rocky Marciano was a heavyweight champion, which hides the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: The final punctuation of the clue is itself the symbol being named, a device setters use for fun.

clue.text: Those practically focused places engulfing boxer

indicators.note: a word engulfing another swallows it whole, so the boxer goes inside

parts.note: to place something is to rest it, so places means rests
Muhammad Ali is the crossword's favourite boxer

explanation.surface: Some locations swallow up a prizefighter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'engulfing' signals the container. 'places' looks like a noun but is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: People who deal with things as they really are, rather than ideals, are pragmatic, practically minded types.

clue.text: New length lines that material

indicators.note: to line something is to sit inside it, so the length goes inside the next word

parts.note: yon is an archaic or dialect word for that

explanation.surface: A fresh stretch of fabric used as a lining.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lines' puts L inside YON. 'lines' looks like a noun but is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: This synthetic polymer is woven into a fabric, an example of a material.

clue.text: Web content of charm, alluring

indicators.note: the content of something sits inside it, so one word fills another

parts.note: charm can mean magic, a spell
the Net is the internet or web

explanation.surface: Online material with some charm proves attractive.
explanation.walkthrough: 'content of' signals the container: the web term sits inside the word for charm. 'Web' looks like part of the definition but is wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Magnetic charm draws people in, a figurative synonym for attractive.

clue.text: G's neighbour secures nothing in business

indicators.note: to secure something is to hold it fast inside, so one piece encloses the other

parts.note: on a keyboard A flat sits next to G
O looks like zero, nothing

explanation.surface: A company boss next to G holds onto nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'secures' puts O inside A FLAT. 'G' looks like a letter of the alphabet, but it is the musical note.
explanation.definitionFit: A firm still afloat is solvent and trading, an idiom for staying in business.

clue.text: Such a testing period building an airport by 1st October

indicators.note: building makes something new out of materials, so the letters are put together afresh
the 1st of a word is its opening letter

explanation.surface: A trial phase for constructing an airport by the start of October.
explanation.walkthrough: 'building' rearranges AN, AIRPORT and BY with O, the 1st letter of October.
explanation.definitionFit: A trial period for a new employee or offender is described by this adjective, the period itself being the test.

clue.text: Frugal type pockets two notes and 50p? Here's another note!

indicators.note: to pocket is to take something inside, so the notes and coin go into the saver

parts.note: a frugal person is a saver
E is one musical note
mi is the third note of the sol-fa scale
50p is half a pound, or half a quid: half the word quid

explanation.surface: A thrifty person stashes some banknotes and a coin, then finds another banknote.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pockets' signals the container round both notes and the coin. 'notes' looks like money but means musical notes; 50p as QU (half a quid) is a stretch the solver must accept.
explanation.definitionFit: This sixteenth note is a short musical note, so it is another note after the two named.

clue.text: Table reference you 'n' I reversed?

parts.note: I, put as the object, becomes me
N stands for 'n', a contraction of and
U is text-speak for you

explanation.surface: A casual 'you and I', flipped round, as a guide at the dining table.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reversed' turns 'you 'n' I' into 'me 'n' you', words in reverse order, not letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A restaurant list of dishes is consulted at the table, a playful sense for a reference.

clue.text: Element finding an Athenian, unknown

parts.note: Timon of Athens is the title character of a Shakespeare play
Y is a mathematical unknown

explanation.surface: Discovering a chemical element with a mysterious Greek.
explanation.definitionFit: Antimony is a metalloid, chemical element number 51, an example of an element.

clue.text: Subject of autobiography writing material on a politician, fascist leader?

definitions.text: Subject of autobiography writing material on a politician, fascist leader?

parts.note: the subject of an autobiography is the writer themselves, me
ink is a material for writing
MP, Member of Parliament, is a politician

indicators.note: the leader of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: A dictator's memoir: its subject writing about himself, a politician and fascist chief.
explanation.walkthrough: 'leader' takes F from fascist. The whole clue also describes Hitler's book, written by a politician who led the fascists.
explanation.definitionFit: Hitler wrote this book about his life and ideology, so it is an autobiography by a fascist leader.

clue.text: Fool the president, promoting mother in Canadian province

indicators.note: promoting moves something up, here to the front in a down answer

parts.note: a nit is a fool, a nitwit
Barack Obama was US president when this was set
Ma is a word for mother

explanation.surface: Making a fool of the president while advancing mum's career in Canada.
explanation.walkthrough: 'promoting' moves MA from the end of NITOBAMA to the top.
explanation.definitionFit: Manitoba is one of the ten provinces of Canada, an example of the category.

clue.text: Great readers left with repetition? That's not on

indicators.note: not on says the word on is missing from the piece

parts.note: an iteration is a repetition

explanation.surface: Avid readers who keep repeating themselves, which just isn't acceptable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'That's not' removes ON from ITERATION, leaving ITERATI. 'not on' looks like 'unacceptable'.
explanation.definitionFit: The literati are well-read, educated people, great readers in the literary sense.

clue.text: I am (ungrammatically) cross as a goat

parts.note: 'I be' is a nonstandard way of saying I am
a cross is the letter X

explanation.surface: Speaking badly, I am as angry as a goat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cross' looks like 'angry' but is the letter X.
explanation.definitionFit: The ibex is a wild mountain goat with long curved horns, an example of a goat.

clue.text: Setter, perhaps, seeking a number under a hundred

indicators.note: in a down answer, under means placed below the following piece

parts.note: C is the Roman numeral for a hundred
nine is a number

explanation.surface: A crossword compiler hunting for a figure below one hundred.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Setter' looks like the crossword compiler, but it is the dog: setters are gundogs.
explanation.definitionFit: A setter is a breed of dog, so it is an example of something doglike, hence 'perhaps'.

clue.text: Force some tin, opening low-fat cheese?

indicators.note: opening up a word lets another piece in, so the cheese is split around the letters

parts.note: quark is a soft, low-fat curd cheese

indicators.note: to force something is to bend it out of shape, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Prising open some tin of low-fat cheese, are we?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Force' rearranges the seven letters of the two short words; 'opening' splits the cheese around them. The definition is the printed punctuation mark at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: The clue's final punctuation is itself the symbol meant, a trick paired with the exclamation clue.

clue.text: Tie bits up

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the letters are read from the bottom

parts.note: bits are parts

explanation.surface: Fasten the pieces together.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' turns PARTS backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A strap is a band used to fasten or tie things, and to strap is to tie.

clue.text: Tail of rabbits, shortened

indicators.note: the tail of a word is its last letter

parts.note: cut means shortened

explanation.surface: A rabbit's fluffy rear, cut short.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tail of' takes S from rabbits. The whole clue also describes the answer: a scut is a short tail, as on a rabbit.
explanation.definitionFit: A scut is the short, stubby tail of a rabbit, hare or deer, as the clue describes.

clue.text: Ultimately, renegade left side a lot

indicators.note: ultimately means at the end, so the last letter is taken

parts.note: the verso is the left-hand page of an open book

explanation.surface: In the end, the deserter left a great deal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ultimately' takes E from renegade.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means very or greatly, as in thanking someone a lot.

clue.text: Steep aim, but wild, reaching companion

indicators.note: wild means out of control, so the letters are scattered

parts.note: CH is Companion of Honour, a British order

explanation.surface: A tall target, but uncontrolled, reaching a friend.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wild' rearranges AIM and BUT. 'Steep' looks like a slope but means excessive.
explanation.definitionFit: Steep can mean excessive or unreasonable, like a price, an idiomatic synonym.

clue.text: Fall behind, so taste second

parts.note: a drop is a small taste of a drink
to second a motion is to back it

explanation.surface: Lag behind, so sample the next helping.
explanation.walkthrough: 'second' looks like a noun but is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To fail to keep up with the pack is to lag behind, a phrasal-verb synonym.

clue.text: Weakened party after election finds openings

indicators.note: after places the party at the end
openings of words are their first letters

parts.note: a fete is a festive party

explanation.surface: A feeble party after the vote discovers some job opportunities.
explanation.walkthrough: 'openings' takes E and F from election and finds.
explanation.definitionFit: Effete means feeble or exhausted, a synonym for weakened.
